prompt: A Go file has a C function in a comment, then a blank line, then `import "C"`. The build says `C.mean` is undefined. Why?
hint: The documentation's word for where the comment must be is "immediately".

choices.text: Separated by that line, it is no longer the preamble, so none of it is compiled as C
choices.why: Right. Only a comment immediately before the import is the preamble; separated by a blank line, it is just a comment and nothing in it is compiled as C.

choices.text: C function names must start with a capital letter to be visible from Go
choices.why: The documentation says every name declared in the preamble may be used, even one that starts with a lower-case letter.

choices.text: `static` functions in the preamble cannot be called from Go
choices.why: Static functions are permitted; it is static variables that Go may not reference. `mean` in section 02 was static.

choices.text: gcc is missing, so cgo skipped the comment
choices.why: Without a compiler cgo is off and the file importing `"C"` is left out of the build altogether, which gives a different error.

prompt: To link the C maths library, the preamble carries the directive `#cgo ___: -lm`.
hint: The variable of the same family that you would set in the environment is `CGO_` plus this word.

prompt: `go build` fails with `cannot use total (variable of type int) as C.long value in argument to (C.mean)`. What is the fix?
hint: Go never converts between numeric types on its own, and a C type is a Go type.

choices.text: Declare `total` as `int64`, which is the same size as a C `long` here
choices.why: An `int64` is still not a `C.long`: they are distinct types even where the bits agree, so the error would only change its wording.

choices.text: Pass `C.long(total)`
choices.why: Right. Every value crosses with an explicit conversion into the C type the declaration asks for.

choices.text: Change the C function to take `int`, which cgo maps to Go's `int`
choices.why: `C.int` is its own Go type, 4 bytes on this machine, and Go's `int` is 8. The error would name `C.int` instead.

choices.text: Add `#cgo CFLAGS: -std=gnu99`, so that gcc accepts the call
choices.why: The error comes from the Go compiler checking the call against the preamble's declaration; gcc never sees it.

prompt: Put the commands `go build -x` printed for `first`'s package in the order they ran.
hint: Nothing can be compiled as Go until the file has been split, and the link comes last.
items: `cgo` splits main.go into a Go half and a C half
`gcc -c` compiles the C half and the files cgo generated
`gcc` links those objects with `-lm`, to learn which symbols come from shared libraries
`cgo -dynout` writes that list down as Go
`link -extld=gcc` links the program, with gcc doing the final step

prompt: `gzlines` prints `C.GoString(C.zlibVersion())`. Who frees the C string that `zlibVersion` returned?
hint: Ask who allocated it.

choices.text: `gzlines`, with `C.free`, right after `C.GoString` copies it
choices.why: Only memory you allocated, like a `C.CString`, is yours to free. Freeing zlib's own string hands memory that was never `malloc`ed to `free`.

choices.text: The garbage collector, once the Go copy is unreachable
choices.why: The collector frees the Go string `C.GoString` made. It does not know the C string exists.

choices.text: Nobody: zlib owns it
choices.why: Right. It points into zlib's own memory. The program copies it into Go and leaves the original alone.

choices.text: `gzclose`, which releases everything zlib allocated for the file
choices.why: `gzclose` frees the `gzFile` and its state. `zlibVersion` has nothing to do with any file.

prompt: Match each value from section 03 with what releases it.
hint: One of them is not memory C allocated at all.

prompt: Which of these follow the pointer-passing rules, with cgocheck on and no `runtime.Pinner`? Choose every one that does.
hint: The question each time: is it Go memory, and does that memory hold a Go pointer?

choices.text: Passing `&buf[0]` of a `[]byte` to a C function that reads it and returns
choices.why: Allowed: Go memory with no Go pointers inside, lent for the length of the call.

choices.text: Passing `&s`, a Go variable of a C struct type whose `data` field holds a pointer from `C.CString`
choices.why: Allowed: `s` is Go memory, but the pointer inside it is a C pointer, which the collector does not manage.

choices.text: Passing `&s` whose `data` field points into a Go `[]byte`
choices.why: That is `rules/main.go`: Go memory holding a pointer to unpinned Go memory, and the runtime panicked on the call.

choices.text: A C function storing the `&buf[0]` it was given in a global, to read it on the next call
choices.why: C may not keep a Go pointer after the call returns unless the memory is pinned, and here it is not.

prompt: With `GODEBUG=cgocheck=0`, `rules` printed `10` and exit status 0. What does that run show?
hint: What was turned off, and what did the program happen to do before anything could go wrong?

choices.text: That the panic was a false alarm, since the right answer came out
choices.why: The rule was broken either way. The answer was right because nothing moved `line` during a call that short.

choices.text: That `span_len` copied the bytes, so no Go pointer reached C
choices.why: `span_len` read the `len` field of a struct whose `data` still pointed into Go memory; nothing was copied.

choices.text: Only that the check was off: the violation is still there and fails the day the collector runs at the wrong moment
choices.why: Right. Turning the check off removes the alarm, not the bug; the fix is to pin `line` or to keep Go pointers out of what C receives.

choices.text: That cgocheck only applies to builds made with `-race`
choices.why: The check is on by default as `GODEBUG=cgocheck=1` in every build; it caught `rules` in an ordinary one.

prompt: In the run in section 04, `BenchmarkGoAdd1` took 0.7894 ns/op and `BenchmarkCAdd1` took 28.70 ns/op. To the nearest whole number, how many times longer did the call into C take?
hint: Divide the C figure by the Go one.

prompt: Moving the per-line loop into C cut 20,000 crossings to one, yet saved 0.26 ms out of 2.12 ms rather than the 0.57 ms that 20,000 × 28.70 ns predicts. What explains the gap?
hint: What else happens in each of those 20,000 calls?

choices.text: cgocheck inspects every pointer argument, and the per-line version has more of them
choices.why: cgocheck runs on the per-line calls too, and the benchmark of `add1`, which passes no pointer, still costs 28.70 ns.

choices.text: Each call also does about 90 ns of `crc32` work, so the empty-function price is a ceiling here
choices.why: Right. The crossing measured on an empty function is the worst case; next to real work in every call, what batching saves is smaller.

choices.text: gcc inlined `crc32` into `crc_lines`, which made the C loop slower
choices.why: `crc32` lives in `libz.so.1`, a shared library, and gcc cannot inline across that boundary.

choices.text: The C loop computes a different checksum, so the two are not comparable
choices.why: The benchmark checks every version against `hash/crc32` before timing it, and all four agreed.

prompt: A web service calls a C function that waits up to two seconds on a hardware device, once in every request handler. Under 300 requests at once, what does section 04 predict?
hint: Section 04 counted threads, not goroutines.

choices.text: About 300 goroutines parked and the same few threads, as with any blocking call in Go
choices.why: That is what `time.Sleep` did: 6 threads. A goroutine waiting inside C holds its thread, as `usleep` showed with 104.

choices.text: Requests queue behind GOMAXPROCS threads, so at most 4 wait at once
choices.why: The scheduler starts a new thread whenever one disappears into C, precisely so that Go code keeps running; nothing caps it at GOMAXPROCS.

choices.text: Around 300 operating system threads, one held by each waiting request
choices.why: Right. 100 goroutines asleep in C gave 104 threads; 300 waiting in C give roughly 300, a thread count that follows the traffic.

choices.text: The runtime panics after cgocheck detects a blocking call
choices.why: cgocheck checks pointers passed to C. A C function is free to block, and the runtime pays for it with a thread.

prompt: `ldd bin/gzlines` lists `libz.so.1`. You copy `gzlines` to a server that has no zlib installed. What happens?
hint: Who reads that list, and when?

choices.text: It runs, because Go copied zlib into the binary when it linked
choices.why: That is `gzlines-static`, built with `-extldflags=-static`. The plain build only records that it needs `libz.so.1`.

choices.text: It starts, and fails with a Go error at the first call to `gzopen`
choices.why: The library is looked for before `main` starts, by the loader, not at the call.

choices.text: The loader cannot find `libz.so.1`, and `gzlines` never starts
choices.why: Right. A dynamically linked binary needs every library `ldd` lists on the machine that runs it.

choices.text: It falls back to `compress/gzip`, as `os/user` falls back to `/etc/passwd`
choices.why: That fallback is chosen at build time inside the standard library. `gzlines` has no pure Go half to fall back on.

prompt: `CGO_ENABLED=1 GOARCH=arm64 CC=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc go build ./gzlines` stopped because that compiler is not installed. If it were installed, what else would the build need?
hint: The C half has to be linked, for ARM, against the C libraries it uses.

choices.text: Nothing: with a cross compiler named in `CC`, cgo builds for ARM
choices.why: The compiler is one piece. Linking needs ARM's C library and an ARM `libz` as well.

choices.text: The C library's headers and libraries for ARM, and an ARM build of zlib
choices.why: Right. Every C library the program uses has to exist for the target, which is why each one multiplies the work.

choices.text: `qemu-aarch64-static`, to run gcc for ARM on this machine
choices.why: qemu runs the finished ARM binary. A cross compiler is an ordinary x86-64 program that writes ARM code.

choices.text: `CGO_ENABLED=0`, so that the file importing `"C"` is compiled as Go
choices.why: With cgo off the file is left out entirely, which is the `build constraints exclude all Go files` error.

prompt: A release job builds a service that stores its data with go-sqlite3, using `CGO_ENABLED=0` for static binaries. The build and the unit tests that do not open a database pass. What happens in production?
hint: go-sqlite3 has a file for builds without cgo.

choices.text: The build fails with `build constraints exclude all Go files`
choices.why: That is what happens to a package with no Go files left, like `gzlines`. go-sqlite3 ships a stub precisely so that its importers still compile.

choices.text: The binary is static and uses a pure Go SQLite bundled as a fallback
choices.why: There is no fallback engine in go-sqlite3; the stub only refuses. The pure Go port is a different module.

choices.text: It runs, and the first use of the database fails with the stub's message that go-sqlite3 requires cgo
choices.why: Right. `sq-nocgo` built and then exited 1 with `Binary was compiled with 'CGO_ENABLED=0', go-sqlite3 requires cgo to work`.

choices.text: The loader refuses to start it because `libsqlite3.so` is missing
choices.why: go-sqlite3 compiles SQLite into the binary; even the cgo build of `sq` needed only `libc.so.6` and the loader.

prompt: A program uses `net` and `os/user`, and also calls zlib through cgo. It is built with `-tags netgo,osusergo`. What does `file` say about the binary?
hint: What exactly do the two tags switch off?

choices.text: Statically linked, because the tags remove every use of C
choices.why: The tags choose the pure Go halves of those two standard packages. Your own `import "C"` and its `-lz` are untouched.

choices.text: Dynamically linked, since zlib still needs the loader
choices.why: Right. `netgo` and `osusergo` emptied the `CgoFiles` of `net` and `os/user`; they cannot remove C you wrote.

choices.text: The build fails: the tags require `CGO_ENABLED=0`
choices.why: `lookup-pure` was built with the tags while cgo was on, and came out static.

choices.text: Statically linked, but only on a machine without gcc
choices.why: Without gcc, cgo would be off and the zlib file would be left out, so the build would fail rather than come out static.

prompt: In `crash`, the same `try` with the same deferred `recover` caught the Go nil dereference and not the C one. Why?
hint: Read the third line the program printed.

choices.text: `recover` only works in the goroutine that panicked, and C runs in another one
choices.why: The C call ran in the same goroutine; the dump shows `main.try` calling it.

choices.text: The deferred function was registered after the C call started
choices.why: `defer` ran before `f()` in `try`, for both calls; the difference is in what happened, not in the order.

choices.text: A fault during C code is fatal: the runtime does not turn it into a panic
choices.why: Right. `signal arrived during cgo execution` is the runtime saying it was in C, where it cannot know what state was left, so it stops the whole program.

choices.text: The C function returned an error code that Go ignored
choices.why: `first` never returned; it read through a null pointer and the process received `SIGSEGV`.

prompt: Section 06 lists where to look before writing `import "C"`. Put the options in the order it gives them, first to last.
hint: cgo itself is the last resort.
items: a pure Go port of the C library
the C tool run as a separate process with `os/exec`
cgo, kept in one small package

prompt: `func label(s string) { C.puts(C.CString(s)) }` is called once for each of the 20,000 lines of the log. What is wrong with it?
hint: Count what `C.CString` allocates and what frees it.

choices.text: Every call leaks a C copy of the string, since nothing calls `C.free`
choices.why: Right. `C.CString` mallocs a copy the collector never sees; without `defer C.free(unsafe.Pointer(cs))` each line leaks one.

choices.text: It breaks the pointer rules: `puts` receives a Go pointer
choices.why: `C.CString` returns a C pointer to C memory, which may be passed freely.

choices.text: The garbage collector may free the C string while `puts` is printing it
choices.why: The collector does not manage C memory at all, which is the root of the real problem: nobody frees it.

choices.text: It is correct but slow; the only problem is 20,000 crossings
choices.why: The crossings cost about half a millisecond in all. The leak grows with every line for as long as the process runs.

prompt: To hand a Go map to a C library that calls back with an integer of user data, wrap it with `cgo.___(counts)`, and delete it when C is done.
hint: The function from `runtime/cgo` that returns a `Handle`.

prompt: A team wants SHA-256 checksums of uploaded files and proposes calling OpenSSL through cgo, "because C is faster". Which response follows from this lesson?
hint: Think of what happened when zlib's crc32 met `hash/crc32`.

choices.text: Agree, and batch the calls so that each crossing hashes a whole file
choices.why: Batching is the right shape once cgo is chosen, but the lesson's order puts the standard library first, and `crypto/sha256` is in it.

choices.text: Agree, provided the binary is linked statically with `-extldflags=-static`
choices.why: Static linking fixes one cost out of several: cross-compiling, build time and C crashes would remain, for a hash the standard library computes.

choices.text: Measure `crypto/sha256` first: `hash/crc32` beat zlib nine times over
choices.why: Right. The standard library is first on the list and "C is faster" was measured false once already; cgo's costs are only worth paying for something you cannot get otherwise.

choices.text: Refuse: cgo cannot pass a file's contents to C without breaking the pointer rules
choices.why: A `[]byte` holds no Go pointers, so `&data[0]` may be lent to C for a call, as `gzread` and `crc32` were lent theirs.
